head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: After sorting, the median is the middle element `nums[len // 2]` (for an even length this is the UPPER median, as the problem defines)
Moving the median element itself to `k`
Elements left of the median must stay ≤ the median; any that are larger than `k` have to be lowered to `k`
Keep the order consistent with the new median
Elements right of the median must stay ≥ `k`; any smaller ones are raised to `k`

p: `nums = [2,5,6,8,5]` sorts to `[2,5,5,6,8]`, `k = 4`, median position 2:

blocks.h: Why do only the elements on the wrong side need fixing?
p: Once the middle element becomes `k`, the sorted order is preserved as long as everything to its left is ≤ `k` and everything to its right is ≥ `k`. Elements that already satisfy that cost nothing, and the cheapest repair for a violator is to move it exactly to `k`.

3107.takeaway: Make the median equal to k: sort, change the middle element to k, and clamp any elements that fall on the wrong side of k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A monotonic (non-increasing) stack of values, each with how many times it has appeared as the potential LEFT boundary
Smaller values can never again be the maximum of a subarray that reaches `x` or beyond, so drop them
An earlier equal value: the number of valid left boundaries grows by one
The count on top is the number of subarrays ending at this element whose boundary elements are both the maximum (including the one-element subarray)

p: A subarray qualifies when its first and last elements equal the subarray's maximum. For a fixed right end `x`, valid left ends are the earlier positions holding the same value `x` with nothing larger between them. The stack keeps exactly those equal values grouped into one count, and larger values clear the smaller ones away. A brute-force check agreed on random arrays.

3113.takeaway: Subarrays with maximum at both ends: a non-increasing monotonic stack of (value, count); each element adds the count of equal earlier maxima to the answer.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of bits in the binary form of `n` (for 7 = `111` it is 3)
The highest power of two not exceeding `n`
One less than that power of two: a number with all lower bits set

p: Values of `n` and the answer (the largest `x ≤ n` such that `x & (x+1) & … & n == 0`):

blocks.h: Why is the answer one less than the top power of two?
p: If `x` is below the top bit of `n` and `x + 1 ... n` includes the power of two `P = 2^(bit_length−1)` itself, the AND of the range contains `P`, which has a 1 only in the top bit, and numbers below `P` have 0 there: the AND clears everything once the range crosses `P`. The largest `x` that still makes the range cross `P` is `P − 1`. Checked against brute force for every `n < 200`.

3125.takeaway: Largest x whose AND with the rest up to n is zero: it is the highest power of two not above n, minus one.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Each data centre is independent: iterate its four numbers together
If we upgrade `x` servers and sell the other `c − x`, we need `u·x ≤ money + s·(c − x)`
Selling the rest funds the upgrades
The largest integer `x` satisfying it (floor division)
Integer solution of a linear inequality
Cannot upgrade more servers than exist

p: Two data centres:

Selling a server only adds money, and a server that isn't upgraded has no other use, so the best plan sells all of them. Then the number of upgrades is limited only by the money: the inequality above. The formula was checked against a brute force over `x`.

3155.takeaway: Upgradable servers: selling every non-upgraded server funds upgrades, so x ≤ (c·sell + money) / (upgrade + sell), capped at c.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Positions of obstacles in sorted order (position 0 is a sentinel); binary search finds neighbours of a position
Predecessor / successor in a sorted list
`tree[pos]` stores the GAP between the obstacle at `pos` and the previous obstacle; the tree answers 'largest gap among obstacles at positions 0..last' in O(log n)
Range maximum query with point updates
type 1: `update(x, x - prev)` and `update(next, next - x)`
A new obstacle at `x` splits the gap of the next obstacle: its own gap becomes `x − prev`, and the next obstacle's gap shrinks to `next − x`
The last obstacle at or before `x`
Largest gap between obstacles up to `last`, or the open stretch from `last` to `x`
The final stretch isn't an obstacle gap yet
A block of size `sz` fits in `[0, x]` iff some gap is at least `sz`

p: Queries `[1,2]`, `[2,3,3]`, `[2,3,1]`, `[2,2,2]` (place obstacle at 2; can a size-3, size-1, size-2 block fit within `[0, x]`):

head: Query
Obstacles
Result
rows: can a block of size 3 fit in [0, 3]?
can a block of size 1 fit in [0, 3]?
can a block of size 2 fit in [0, 2]?

p: Placing obstacles changes gaps; asking about the largest gap in a prefix needs a range maximum that supports updates. A plain array would make each query O(n). The tree gives O(log n) for both. The code was checked against a brute force on random query sequences.

head: Approach
Per query
rows: O(log n) plus the list insertion

bullets: Time: O(q log q) overall (list insertion is O(q) per insert in the worst case).

3161.takeaway: Block placement: keep sorted obstacles, store each obstacle's gap to its predecessor in a segment tree, and answer a query with the largest gap in the prefix (or the final open stretch).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A letter, followed by its count
The count can have several digits (`c10`), so scan to the end of the digits
Add the count to that letter's total (the same letter can appear several times)

p: The letters sorted are `a`, `b`, `c` with totals 3, 2, 10: `a3b2c10`.

blocks.h: Why parse digits with a loop?
p: Counts may have more than one digit, so you can't just read the next character. Scanning until the first non-digit finds the whole number, and slicing converts it with `int`.

3167.takeaway: Better compression: parse letter-count tokens (multi-digit counts), add counts per letter in a Counter, and output the letters alphabetically.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A min-heap keyed by the letter, then by NEGATIVE index so that among equal letters the one with the LARGEST index comes out first
Remove the smallest letter among those before the star; the star removes it
Each star removes the smallest letter to its left
Indices already removed (we only mark them, and rebuild the string at the end)
Removing a LATER copy of a letter keeps earlier copies in front, which makes the remaining string lexicographically smaller

p: `s = "aaba*"`:

head: Index
Char
Action
Removed indices
rows: remove the smallest letter, rightmost on ties → index 3 ('a')

blocks.h: Why remove the rightmost smallest letter?
p: The problem says each star deletes the smallest letter to its left; when several copies tie, the choice is ours. Deleting the rightmost copy leaves the other copies closer to the front, and for equal letters that gives the smallest remaining string. The result was checked against a brute force over all tie choices.

3170.takeaway: Remove stars lexicographically smallest: a min-heap of (letter, −index); each star pops the smallest letter, preferring the rightmost on ties.

Bitwise OR: a bit is 1 if it is 1 in either number

p: `nums[1:]` is the array shifted by one, so zipping aligns each element with its right neighbour. `zip` stops at the shorter list, which gives exactly `n − 1` pairs, with no index arithmetic.

head: Approach

rows: no indices, copies the list once

3173.takeaway: OR of adjacent elements: zip the array with itself shifted by one and OR each pair.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Longest good subsequence ENDING at index `i` that has at most `j` places where adjacent chosen elements differ
DP (Dynamic Programming) over (end index, allowed changes)
A single element is a subsequence of length 1 with 0 changes
Extend a subsequence ending at `p` with the same value: no new change used
Extend with a different value: one change is used, so look at `j − 1`

p: The longest good subsequence has length 4 (for example `1, 2, 1, 1`, which has two places where adjacent chosen elements differ).

blocks.h: Why is the DP O(n² k)?
p: For each of the `n` end points and each of `k + 1` change budgets, we scan all earlier positions `p`. That is fine for this problem's small `n` (up to 500). The harder version (3177) speeds the inner scan up with a dictionary of best lengths per value.

3176.takeaway: Longest good subsequence with at most k changes: DP on (end index, changes used), extending from earlier positions with the same value for free or a different value at the cost of one change.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Work on a copy so the caller's list is not changed
Scan left to right; a window of three starting at `i` needs `i + 2` to exist
The leftmost zero can ONLY be fixed by a flip that starts at `i` (earlier flips are already decided)
Greedy: fix the first unfixed element
XOR (exclusive OR) with 1 flips a bit
The last two elements can't be the start of a window; if they are not both 1 afterwards, it is impossible

blocks.h: Why is the leftmost-zero greedy forced?
p: Position `i` can only be changed by flips that start at `i − 2`, `i − 1` or `i`. Flips starting before `i` have already been decided, so if `nums[i]` is still 0, the flip starting at `i` is the only remaining way to fix it. So each decision is forced and the count is minimal. A brute force over all flip subsets agreed on random arrays.

3191.takeaway: Binary array to all ones with 3-element flips: scan left to right and flip a window whenever the leftmost element is 0; if the last two are not 1, it is impossible.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Area of the smallest rectangle that covers every 1 inside the given sub-grid (0 if it has no 1s)
Bounding box of the ones in a region
three vertical cuts, three horizontal cuts
Split the grid into 3 strips: two cut lines in the same direction
one vertical cut + one horizontal cut on a side
Split once vertically, then split one of the two halves horizontally: four orientations in total
The remaining partition shapes (an L-shaped arrangement of 3 rectangles)
The smallest total area over all ways to cut the grid into 3 non-empty parts

p: `grid = [[1,0,1],[1,1,1]]`: the best split uses three vertical strips.

Three non-overlapping rectangles that cover a rectangular region and are each a bounding box can be arranged only as three parallel strips (rows or columns) or as one strip plus a perpendicular split of the remainder. The code tries every cut position for each shape. It was checked against a brute force over all triples of disjoint rectangles on random small grids.

head: Shape
Cuts
rows: vertical cut, then split one side horizontally
horizontal cut, then split one side vertically

bullets: Time: O((m + n)² · m · n) in the worst case, because each `area` call scans its region.

3197.takeaway: Cover all ones with three rectangles: try every way to cut the grid into three parts (three strips, or a strip plus a perpendicular split) and sum the bounding-box areas.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Height of the triangle if the first row (1 ball) is colour A and rows alternate: odd rows use colour A, even rows use colour B
The colour of row 1 can be either, so try both
Row number = number of balls in that row (1, 2, 3, …)
Not enough balls of the required colour: stop; the height is `row − 1`
Stop when a row can't be completed
Best of the two starting colours

p: `red = 2`, `blue = 4`:

Rows alternate colours, so odd rows draw from one colour and even rows from the other. A simple loop that subtracts `row` from the right colour until it runs out finds the height in O(√n). Either starting colour may be better, hence the two calls.

3200.takeaway: Maximum triangle height: simulate rows (row r needs r balls of alternating colours) for both starting colours and take the larger height.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Returns the node farthest from `src` and its distance; BFS processes nodes in order of distance, so the last node dequeued is the farthest
Farthest node in an unweighted tree
Two BFS passes: the farthest node from any start is an end of a diameter; the farthest node from THAT end gives the diameter length `d`
Tree diameter in two BFS runs
The radius of a tree with diameter `d`: the best centre is `⌈d/2⌉` away from the farthest node
Connect the centres of the two trees
Longest path through the new edge when joined at both centres: radius + 1 + radius
The merged tree's path crossing the bridge
The new diameter is the largest of the old diameters and the path across the bridge

p: Tree 1 is a star with centre 0 and three leaves (diameter 2); tree 2 is a single edge (diameter 1).

After adding one edge between the two trees, the longest path either stays inside one tree or crosses the new edge. A path across has length (distance from the chosen node in tree 1 to its farthest node) + 1 + (the same in tree 2). The distance to the farthest node is minimised by the tree's centre, equal to ⌈d/2⌉. A brute force over every possible connecting pair agreed on random trees.

head: Approach
Time
rows: try every pair of connecting nodes

3203.takeaway: Minimum diameter after merging two trees: connect their centres; the answer is max(d1, d2, ⌈d1/2⌉ + ⌈d2/2⌉ + 1), with diameters from two BFS runs.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The earliest second at which you may START moving into room `(a, b)`
Wait until the room opens if needed, then spend 1 second moving in
Min-heap by arrival time: Dijkstra's algorithm (shortest paths with non-negative costs)
The first time the destination is popped, it has the earliest arrival

blocks.h: Why Dijkstra and not BFS (Breadth-First Search)?
p: Edge costs depend on time: entering a room costs `max(t, open time) + 1 − t`, which varies. Plain BFS assumes every edge costs 1. Arrival times are non-decreasing along a path, so Dijkstra's greedy choice (always expand the earliest arrival) stays correct.

3341.takeaway: Earliest arrival to the last room: Dijkstra where the cost of stepping into a room is max(current time, room opening time) + 1.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Using only the first `k` queries, can every `nums[i]` be reduced to 0?
Difference array: add `v` of available decrement to every index in `[l, r]` in O(1)
`cur += diff[i]; if cur < nums[i]: return False`
The total decrement available at `i` (each query may decrement by UP TO its value, any amount) must be at least `nums[i]`
If even all queries are not enough, impossible
More queries only add capacity, so `ok` is False…False True…True

p: `nums = [2,0,2]`, `queries = [[0,2,1],[0,2,1],[1,1,3]]`. `cover` is the decrement capacity at each index using the first `mid` queries:

blocks.h: Why can we treat each query as capacity?
p: A query may subtract any amount from 0 up to `v` at each index in its range, independently per index. So the maximum total decrement at an index is the sum of `v` over the queries covering it, and the array can be zeroed exactly when that sum is at least the element. No scheduling is needed.

3356.takeaway: Zero array transformation II: binary search the number of queries; feasibility uses a difference array of total decrement capacity per index.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `n − 2` special numbers, one number that is their SUM, and one outlier
Total = (special sum) + (sum element) + outlier = 2 · (sum element) + outlier
If `s` is the sum element, the outlier must be `total − 2s`
The candidate outlier must actually be in the array
If the outlier equals the sum element's value, the value must appear at least twice (they are different positions)
Several candidates may work; the answer is the LARGEST outlier

p: With `s = 5` the outlier is `20 − 10 = 10`, which is in the array: the special numbers are `2` and `3` (sum 5). The answer is 10. Checked against a brute force over all choices of sum element and outlier.
We need O(1) membership and a way to know whether a value occurs twice. A Counter provides both, so each candidate sum element is tested in O(1), for O(n) overall.

3371.takeaway: Largest outlier: with total T and sum element s, the outlier is T − 2s; check it exists (as a different element) with a Counter and keep the maximum.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many times letter `i` (a = 0 … z = 25) occurs
In a good string every letter that appears has the SAME count `f`; try each `f` from 1 to `n`

Minimum operations after processing the letters so far, where `carry` extra characters are being passed on to the NEXT letter by changing them into it (a change costs 1, while delete + insert would cost 2)
Pass-the-surplus DP (Dynamic Programming) over the alphabet
Count of letter `i` including the `x` characters carried in from the previous letter
Too many: delete the extra, or pass up to `min(ex, need)` of them forward (`need` = how many the next letter lacks)
Surplus moves forward or is deleted
Too few: insert the missing ones
delete everything: cost `t` (or carry some forward)
A letter may also end with count 0
The letter disappears from the string
Nothing can be carried past `z` (it has no next letter)

p: `s = "aaabc"` (`a`: 3, `b`: 1, `c`: 1). The cost for each target frequency `f`:

blocks.p: The best target is `f = 1` with cost 2: for `"aaabc"` the cheapest fix is to delete two `a`s (giving `abc`, each letter once). The DP was checked against a breadth-first search over operation sequences on small strings.

p: A change moves a character to the NEXT letter, so surplus characters can only flow forward through the alphabet. That makes the problem a left-to-right DP where the state is how many characters are passed on. Without it, every combination of insert, delete and change would have to be tried.

bullets: Time: O(n · 26 · states) — roughly O(26 · n²) in the worst case.

3389.takeaway: Make character frequencies equal: for each target frequency run a left-to-right DP over the alphabet, where surplus characters are deleted or passed (changed) to the next letter.
